Synopsis

Three malicious node-ipc npm releases were published on 2026-05-14 after the dormant `atiertant` co-maintainer account was recovered via an expired email domain. The obfuscated payload harvested developer, cloud, SSH, and CI/CD secrets and exfiltrated them over DNS TXT queries.

Story

This is a new node-ipc supply-chain event, separate from the 2022 protestware incident. On 2026-05-14 the npm package took three new releases across active and legacy version lines. 12.0.1 was published at 14:25:30 UTC, 9.2.3 at 14:26:01, and 9.1.6 at 14:26:25. All three were signed by the dormant co-maintainer `atiertant`, inside a 56-second window. Socket traced the entry to expired email domain takeover. The attacker re-registered the lapsed domain behind the maintainer's account, ran a standard npm password reset, and reached publish without touching the project's GitHub repository or any active maintainer's machine. Socket's scanner flagged the publishes within three minutes.

Static comparison against 12.0.0 showed the main ESM file unchanged. All three tarballs had an identical 80 KB obfuscated block appended to `node-ipc.cjs` after the legitimate exports, which made CommonJS consumers the execution path. The payload fired via `setImmediate()` during module load, was exported under `__ntRun`, and forked a detached child marked `__ntw=1`, which served as both an anti-re-execution flag and a process tag. The collector covered 113 paths on Linux and 127 on macOS, including SSH keys, AWS, Azure, and GCP credentials, `.npmrc`, `.env` files, Kubernetes and Docker configs, npm tokens, database connection strings, and AI tool configs including `.claude.json` and `.kiro/settings/mcp.json`. It also captured the full process environment and host details from `uname` and `/etc/hosts`.

Output staged under `<tmpdir>/nt-<pid>/`. The collector tarred the staged data with every file timestamped 1985-10-26, HMAC-signed the archive with the embedded key `qZ8pL3vNxR9wKmTyHbVcFgDsJaEoUi`, and exfiltrated over DNS TXT queries against the `bt.node.js` zone using the prefixes `xh`, `xd`, and `xf` in a custom base-16 reversed-nibble encoding. Bootstrap name resolution went through `sh.azurestaticprovider.net` on port 443 at 37.16.75.69, a deliberate Azure-domain masquerade. DNS-only exfiltration bypassed CI egress controls that would have caught an outbound HTTPS POST.

The package still looked like node-ipc. The name, repository metadata, README, certificates, and API files were intact. The trust break was in the registry distribution channel, where a fresh install or a permissive semver range could resolve to the malicious release without a downstream code review. dist-tags pointed `latest` to 12.0.1, so unversioned installs picked up the malicious build until npm pulled the releases.
